explanations.explanation: Kadesh-barnea is where they arrive. The text says that after the vast and terrifying wilderness, they reached it. It's also where Moses speaks to them about the hill country. Hang on to that name, baker, because it comes back at the end of the passage.

Hazeroth doesn't show up in Moses' retelling here. The text says that after the vast and terrifying wilderness, they reached Kadesh-barnea. That's the stop where Moses speaks to them. Place names run together fast in a long speech, so no worries, friend.

Rephidim isn't the place Moses names in this passage. After the vast and terrifying wilderness, the text says they reached Kadesh-barnea. That's where he tells them about the hill country of the Amorites. Mixing up desert stops is easy, because they all sound like somewhere you'd need a hat.

Moses says no such thing here. He tells them, “Go up and take possession of it as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you.” There's no waiting around for a sign in that line. The land is placed before them and the word is go.

Right, he never tells them to wait for a sign. What he says is, “See, the LORD your God has placed the land before you.” Then comes the order to go up and take possession of it, as the LORD has told them. That's a go-up kind of speech, and I'd be bouncing on my base, ready to roll.
Moses says, “Do not be afraid or discouraged.” He says it right after telling them the land is placed before them. Fear is the word to watch in this passage, baker. It keeps coming back.

Greedy isn't the word Moses uses. He says, “Do not be afraid or discouraged.” I think fear is what he has on his mind here, not wanting too much. Keep that in mind, because fear keeps coming back in this story.
Moses doesn't say careless. His words are, “Do not be afraid or discouraged.” He's talking to people who are about to step into a big, scary job. Fear is the thing he names, friend.

explanations.answer: Word on which route and cities to take
explanations.explanation: The people ask for men who will “…bring us word of what route to follow and which cities to enter.” They want directions, plain and simple. It sounds like a very reasonable ask to me. I'd want a map too, and I'd want it laminated.

explanations.answer: A peace treaty with the Amorite kings
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks for a handshake with the Amorites, friend. The people want men to search out the land and bring word of the route and the cities. Sending back a peace treaty when someone asked for directions is like asking me the oven temperature and getting a whole cookie box.

explanations.answer: Gifts from the people of the land
explanations.explanation: Nobody's asking for a welcome basket. The people want men to search out the land and report on the route and which cities to enter. These scouts are checking the neighborhood before anyone moves in. Keep going, because something does come back down with them.
Moses says, “…I selected twelve men from among you, one from each tribe.” That's one man for every tribe. He also says the plan seemed good to him.
Seven isn't the number. The text says Moses selected twelve men, one from each tribe. Each tribe gets its own set of eyes on the land. Twelve tribes, twelve men, and the math works out.

Seventy scouts, friend? That's not a spy mission, that's a tour group with matching T-shirts. Moses picks twelve, one from each tribe (Deut 1:23). Each tribe gets one man on the trail, and nobody has to carry a clipboard for seventy.

explanations.answer: Some of the fruit of the land
explanations.explanation: The text says, “They took some of the fruit of the land in their hands, carried it down to us…” So the spies don't come back with only words. They bring proof you can hold. It's hard to argue with something you can pick up.

Weapons aren't what the text puts in their hands. It says the spies “…took some of the fruit of the land in their hands, carried it down to us…” That's the souvenir the verse names. Nothing here says they brought back anything from the Amorites.

Stones from walls aren't in this part of the story. The spies carried down some of the fruit of the land. The walls come up later, when the people are describing what they're afraid of. What the spies hold in their hands is fruit.

Not straight up. After the report, Moses says, “…you were unwilling to go up; you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God.” Then he says they grumbled in their tents. They do go up into the hill country later in the passage, but that comes after the LORD speaks.

Correct, they don't head up at that point. Moses says they were unwilling to go up, and he calls it rebelling against the command of the LORD. The spies had said it was a good land, and the people grumbled in their tents anyway. Keep your ears open, baker, because there's more to hear.

explanations.answer: To hand them over to the Amorites
explanations.explanation: Those are the people's own words. They say the LORD brought them out of Egypt “…to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be annihilated.” They say it in their tents, and they begin with, “Because the LORD hates us…” Moses is retelling what they said.

explanations.answer: To make them servants in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Servants in the wilderness isn't in their complaint. They say the LORD brought them out of Egypt to deliver them into the hand of the Amorites to be annihilated. That's a heavy thing to say out loud. And it's what they said in their tents.

explanations.answer: To scatter them among the nations
explanations.explanation: Scattering isn't what they say. Their words are that the LORD brought them out of Egypt “…to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be annihilated.” It's a very specific fear, and it's aimed at one group of people. Moses repeats it exactly.

True. In their grumbling, the people repeat what their brothers said: “The people are larger and taller than we are…” They add that the cities are large, with walls up to the heavens. The people say their brothers made their hearts melt.

It's true, actually. The people quote their brothers who scouted the land, saying, “The people are larger and taller than we are…” The cities are described as large too. That's the report that made their hearts melt.

explanations.answer: The LORD goes before them and will fight for them
explanations.explanation: Moses says, “The LORD your God, who goes before you, will fight for you…” That's the whole reason. It isn't about how strong Israel is. It's about who's walking in front of them.

explanations.answer: The Amorites will run at the sight of them
explanations.explanation: Moses never says the Amorites will run. His reason is that the LORD their God goes before them and will fight for them. The comfort rests on God, not on how scary Israel looks. Big difference, friend.

explanations.answer: The scouts made the people sound too big
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't argue with the scouts' report at all. He points to the LORD, who goes before them and will fight for them. He also reminds them of what they saw Him do in Egypt. His answer to fear is who God is.

explanations.answer: As a man carries his son
explanations.explanation: Moses says the LORD carried them “…as a man carries his son, all the way by which you traveled until you reached this place.” That's a picture of a father and his boy. I like that picture a lot. And Moses says it covers all the way they traveled.

explanations.answer: As a soldier carries his shield
explanations.explanation: A shield isn't the picture Moses uses. He says the LORD carried them “…as a man carries his son…” It's about a father's care, not about gear. All the way to this very place.

explanations.answer: As a servant carries a load
explanations.explanation: A load isn't the picture. Moses says the LORD carried them in the wilderness “…as a man carries his son…” It's a father and a son, not a servant and a load. And Moses says it covers all the way they traveled until they reached this place.

explanations.answer: In fire by night and cloud by day
explanations.explanation: Fire when it's dark, cloud when it's light, and the LORD goes ahead of them in both. Moses says it's to seek out a place for them to camp and to show them the road to travel. Think about that for a second. Nobody in that camp had to argue about directions.

explanations.answer: Through an angel with a drawn sword
explanations.explanation: An angel with a sword isn't how Moses describes it here. He says the LORD went before them in the fire by night and in the cloud by day. That's the way they were led on the whole journey. Fire when it's dark, cloud when it's light.

explanations.answer: In a bright star each evening
explanations.explanation: A star isn't in Moses' words. He says the LORD went before them in the fire by night and in the cloud by day. Stars are lovely, and I do like to look at mine, but this passage names fire and cloud.

True. Moses says the LORD went before them “…to seek out a place for you to camp and to show you the road to travel.” He picked the camping spots and showed the road. That's a lot of care for people who'd soon refuse to trust Him.

It's true. Moses says the LORD went before them “…to seek out a place for you to camp and to show you the road to travel.” He wasn't only pointing the direction. He was also seeking out places for them to camp.

explanations.answer: Not one of them will see the good land
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “Not one of the men of this evil generation shall see the good land I swore to give your fathers…” That's a hard word, and it comes after He heard their words and grew angry. There's one exception coming, so keep reading.

explanations.answer: They must wait one more year to go in
explanations.explanation: A year of waiting isn't what He swears. The LORD says, “Not one of the men of this evil generation shall see the good land I swore to give your fathers…” That's much heavier than a delay. Only one man is named as an exception.

explanations.answer: They must build cities in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Building cities isn't in the oath. The LORD swears that not one of the men of this evil generation will see the good land He swore to give their fathers. That's the whole sentence, and it's a sober one. It makes the next verse stand out.

The LORD says Caleb son of Jephunneh will see the land “…because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly.” Wholeheartedly means all in. That's the reason the LORD gives for Caleb. He adds that He will give Caleb and his descendants the land on which he has set foot.
Patiently isn't the word. The LORD says Caleb will see the land because he followed Him wholeheartedly. That means all in, nothing held back. Patience is great, but that's not what the text says.
Humbly isn't the word the LORD uses. He says Caleb will see the land “…because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly.” It's about following with everything he had. Keep that one close, baker.
The LORD actually says the opposite to Moses: “Not even you shall enter the land.” Moses tells the people this was on their account. I think this one hurts, friend. It's a heavy part of the speech.

Right. The LORD tells Moses, “Not even you shall enter the land.” Moses says the LORD was angry with him on their account. I think this is a hard thing for him to say out loud, so I'll just let it be heavy for a second.

Encourage is the word. Moses is told to cheer on Joshua son of Nun, the man who will carry the next stretch of the job. I think Moses knows what a heavy load feels like. Anybody facing something huge could use someone in their corner, even a stamper with a worn-down handle.

Test isn't the word. The LORD says, “Encourage him, for he will enable Israel to inherit the land.” Joshua son of Nun is getting a boost, not a quiz. A leader about to carry a big load needs a cheering section.

Warn isn't what the LORD says. The word is “Encourage him, for he will enable Israel to inherit the land.” The LORD says Joshua will enter the land and will enable Israel to inherit it. Moses' instruction is to encourage him.

explanations.answer: They will enter and possess the land
explanations.explanation: The LORD says these little ones “…will enter the land that I will give them, and they will possess it.” These are the children who, in the people's words, would become captives. They didn't know good from evil on that day. And now the promise lands right on them.

explanations.answer: They will grow up back in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't in the promise. The LORD says the children “…will enter the land that I will give them, and they will possess it.” The ones the people feared would become captives are the ones who get the land. That's quite a turnaround.

explanations.answer: They will return to Horeb with Moses
explanations.explanation: Horeb isn't in the LORD's words about the children. He says they will enter the land that He will give them, and they will possess it. The little ones the people worried about are the ones who go in. And Moses, as we just heard, doesn't.

explanations.answer: Back to the wilderness toward the Red Sea
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “But you are to turn back and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea.” So the direction is back toward the wilderness. I think that's a hard order to hear. A turn-around is a turn-around.

explanations.answer: Back to Egypt the way they came
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't named in this order. The LORD tells them to turn back and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea. Egypt is where the LORD brought them out of, but this order points to the wilderness.

explanations.answer: Back to Horeb to wait at the mountain
explanations.explanation: Horeb isn't named in this order. The LORD says to turn back and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea. No waiting at a mountain here. It's the wilderness route that He points them to.

The people say, “We will go up and fight, as the LORD our God has commanded us.” Funny how fast the answer changed, from refusing to go to ready to fight. I think they meant it, but the LORD's command had changed. Their plan didn't match His.
Pray isn't the word they use. They say, “We will go up and fight, as the LORD our God has commanded us.” That's a plan with weapons in it. And each man puts his on right after.

Waiting is the opposite of what they say. They say, “We will go up and fight, as the LORD our God has commanded us.” That's a big switch from staying in their tents. Moses makes sure to tell us each man strapped on his weapons.

True. Moses says each man put on his weapons of war, “…thinking it easy to go up into the hill country.” Earlier the people said the cities had walls up to the heavens. Now they think going up is easy, and I think that's quite a swing.

It's true. The text says each man put on his weapons of war, “…thinking it easy to go up into the hill country.” Compare that with the people earlier saying the cities were large, with walls up to the heavens. Now the thought is that it's easy. That's quite a swing, and I can't help noticing it.

explanations.answer: The LORD is not with them
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “…I am not with you to keep you from defeat by your enemies.” That's the reason He gives for this fight: He is not with them. So He tells them not to go up and fight.
Peace isn't offered anywhere in this passage. The LORD's reason is, “…I am not with you to keep you from defeat by your enemies.” That's the whole thing. Without Him there, they'd be beaten.
Their weapons aren't the issue. The text says each man put his on. The LORD's reason is, “…I am not with you to keep you from defeat by your enemies.” It's about who's with them, not what they carry.

Moses hands over the LORD's warning and gets nothing back, because the people “…would not listen.” Then up into the hill country they go anyway. It's like hearing the oven timer go off and sliding the cookies back in for one more minute. I think that's a lot of confidence for people who were unwilling to go up earlier in the same story (Deut 1:26).

Waiting for another sign isn't in the passage. The text says the people “…would not listen.” They “…presumptuously went up into the hill country.” That's quite a change from a crowd that was unwilling to go up before (Deut 1:26). A second sign never comes up.

explanations.answer: They ask Moses to go first
explanations.explanation: Nothing like that is in the passage. Moses says he spoke to them, they would not listen, and they went up into the hill country. Whether Moses went along isn't something these verses say. What they say is that the people rebelled against the command of the LORD.
Moses says the Amorites “…chased you like a swarm of bees.” They routed Israel from Seir all the way to Hormah. It went just the way the LORD's warning said it would.

It's the other way around. The Amorites came out and chased Israel “…like a swarm of bees.” Israel is the one running, all the way from Seir to Hormah. And a swarm of bees is a bad crowd to be chased by, friend.

Peace isn't what Moses reports. The Amorites who lived in the hills came out against Israel, and the chase ran from Seir to Hormah. Moses says it was “…like a swarm of bees.” I think this part is heavy.

That's not what the text says. Moses says they returned and wept before the LORD, “…but He would not listen to your voice or give ear to you.” It's a sad verse. I think it's heavy, so let's treat it with care.
Right. The people returned and wept before the LORD, but He would not listen to their voice or give ear to them. That's a hard verse to read. I think it stings, and Moses doesn't dress it up.
